analysis.one_liner: Requires federal courts to hold a fresh trial on the facts when an agency tries to penalize someone, instead of deferring to the agency's findings.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require a fresh trial of the facts whenever a federal agency seeks to penalize someone, has no cosponsors and sits in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, when a federal court reviews an agency decision that penalizes someone — a fine, a license revocation, an enforcement order — the court generally accepts the agency's factual findings unless they are unsupported. This bill would change that: whenever an agency action seeks a sanction, the court would have to hold a new trial and decide the facts from scratch, even redoing the evidence developed in the agency's own proceeding. The bill was introduced by Rep. Harriet Hageman with no cosponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone contesting a federal agency sanction — a fine, penalty, or disciplinary action — would get a fresh trial in federal court where the agency must prove its case from scratch. In practice, the parties most likely to use this are regulated businesses and individuals with the resources to litigate, since full trials in federal court are expensive.

how_it_helps.text: It amends the APA so that when an agency action seeks a sanction, the reviewing court decides the facts anew — 'including the product of any rulemaking or adjudication' — rather than deferring to the agency's findings.
This gives anyone facing a federal sanction a full evidentiary hearing in federal court instead of review limited to the agency's record.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies and the public: enforcement cases would become slower and costlier, since each contested sanction would require a full court trial rather than review of the agency's record. Taxpayers bear the court costs, and penalties against violators become harder to sustain.

drawbacks.text: Requiring a full trial of facts in federal court for every sanctioned case would make agency enforcement slower and more expensive, since courts currently rely on the agency's record rather than holding a new trial.
Because parties with more resources can better afford de novo litigation, the change could tilt enforcement outcomes toward well-funded regulated parties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is stronger due-process protection for anyone facing a government sanction — a real safeguard, since agencies win deference in most cases today. The cost is significant: full trials in federal court are slow and expensive, so the change would mainly advantage parties that can afford extended litigation — large companies facing regulatory penalties — while making enforcement slower and weaker overall. As a one-sentence bill with no cosponsors, it is also more a statement of principle than a developed proposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote, and it has no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Harriet Hageman introduced the bill on June 11, 2026, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill has received no further action beyond the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the outcome preserves the status quo: agencies can continue relying on judicial deference to their factual findings, and regulated parties challenging sanctions have not gained the new trial right. Nothing has been decided; the bill simply has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill has not moved

for.name: Rep. Harriet Hageman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require de novo fact-finding when agencies seek sanctions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors from either party, and no vote, so its partisan shape cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Regulated industries facing agency enforcement (finance, energy, environment, drug makers)
industries.note: Any company or individual contesting a federal sanction would get a full new trial on the facts in court, a materially better position than today's deferential review. The practical effect is to make agency penalties harder to sustain.
Enforcement actions would face a higher, slower bar, reducing agency leverage. The agencies themselves keep their statutory authority but lose much of the practical force behind sanctions.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since referral in June 2026, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or markup in the Judiciary Committee, and most bills at this stage never advance further.
